claims.text: Protective oxide development and retention in high-entropy alloys is primarily governed by differential diffusion kinetics of Cr and Al.
Selective surface oxidation of Cr and Al enables rapid formation of a continuous, adherent protective scale.
Equiatomic CoCrFeNiMn is a representative five-element high-entropy alloy for the proposed test.
The initial equiatomic alloy has a disordered, homogeneous solid-solution microstructure before oxidation.
The protective scale has a layered structure containing an inner Cr- or Al-rich oxide layer.
The inner Cr- or Al-rich oxide layer acts as a barrier to further oxygen ingress.
At high temperature, Cr and Al diffuse outward faster than oxygen diffuses inward.
Outward transport of Cr and Al causes their preferential oxidation into a compact, continuous oxide layer.
Protective oxide formation is critically sensitive to Cr or Al concentration and ambient oxygen partial pressure.
Minor changes in Cr or Al concentration can produce a nonuniform or less-adherent oxide film.
An equiatomic baseline alloy under standard oxygen pressure forms a uniform, adherent protective oxide with controlled thickness.
Reducing Cr or Al content will produce thicker, discontinuous, or loosely adherent scales and lower oxidation resistance than the baseline.
Changing oxygen partial pressure from the baseline will produce thicker, discontinuous, or loosely adherent scales and lower oxidation resistance.
The proposed mechanism applies at oxidation temperatures of at least 700 °C.
The proposed mechanism requires sufficient Cr and/or Al in the alloy.
A dense Al-containing oxide film can slow subsequent scale thickening and provide some high-temperature oxidation protection.
In CoCrFeNiMn, oxidation-induced surface evolution is governed by elemental environmental interactions, with redox potential becoming dominant over time.

contradictions.description: The concrete baseline example, equiatomic CoCrFeNiMn, contains no Al, yet the intervention proposes reducing its Al content and the mechanism and prediction repeatedly treat Al as a baseline key element.
